strengths: Addresses an ambitious and under-explored inverse problem in digital human modeling: inferring dynamic 3D muscle deformations directly from observable surface motion and pose.

Introduces the SKIM dataset, combining a custom ArUco-embedded suit captured across a 120-camera markerless capture studio, high-resolution static multi-view scans, and individualized anatomical registrations.

Sound mathematical formulation decoupling the deformation into skeletal-driven muscle bulges and residual skin offsets, with a principled suite of physically inspired priors (e.g., prism-based signed volume preservation, biharmonic bending resistance, and sliding constraints).
Thorough ablation study clearly analyzing the individual roles and trade-offs of the geometric, architectural, and volumetric regularization terms.
weaknesses: Lack of dynamic anatomical ground truth: Because dynamic in-vivo imaging (e.g., dynamic MRI/ultrasound) was not acquired during motion, internal muscle deformations are primarily validated via surface marker reprojection and geometric heuristics rather than direct measurement of real dynamic muscle shapes.

High acquisition overhead and subject-specific limitation: The pipeline relies on specialized multi-view capture setups (120 cameras), high-density static scanners, and a custom fiducial suit for each subject, making generalization across unseen identities currently constrained.

Architectural clarity: In Section 4.1, the paper mentions using a 'non-linear U-Net architecture' to map pose features $r^*(\theta) \in \mathbb{R}^{9(J-1)}$ to vertex displacement fields $D_{musc}$, but lacks concrete details on whether this operates on UV parameterization, graph/mesh convolutions, or voxel grids.
Minor editorial redundancy: On page 9 (bottom of Section 4.2), two consecutive sentences are nearly identical repetitions of each other regarding invariance to global pose in canonical coordinates.

strengths: Addresses an ambitious and underexplored problem in computer vision and graphics: recovering dynamic 3D internal muscle deformations directly from articulated skeletal motion and surface observations.

The SKIM dataset represents a substantial capture effort, combining a dense multi-camera capture setup (120 cameras), high-resolution static body scanning (140 cameras), and a custom ArUco marker suit to obtain accurate surface correspondences and residual dynamic fields.

Well-motivated biomechanical priors and formulation: decomposing deformations into muscle and residual skin layers, coupled with biharmonic bending resistance, tangential anchoring, and Gauss-Legendre prism volume preservation, which effectively regularize an otherwise severely ill-posed inverse problem.
Thorough ablation studies justifying the choice of U-Net architecture and demonstrating the individual necessity of the proposed vector and volumetric regularizations.
weaknesses: Lack of direct in-vivo ground-truth validation for dynamic internal muscle shapes: While skin surface tracking and volume conservation are evaluated, the true internal muscle deformations are not validated against dynamic medical ground truth (e.g., cine-MRI or dynamic ultrasound), leaving internal accuracy reliant on surrogate physical metrics.

Limited generalization and scalability: The method is strictly subject-specific, requiring dense multi-camera capture with a specialized marker suit and individualized static anatomical fitting for each person, limiting immediate applicability to in-the-wild or general multi-subject scenarios.

Baseline comparisons are somewhat limited: HIT was primarily designed for static implicit shape estimation rather than dynamic performance capture, leading to an unfair comparison on dynamic tracking metrics. Comparing against dynamic physics-based skinning or neural FEM approximations (e.g., Han et al., 2024 or Fast Projective Skinning) would have provided stronger context.

Clarity on evaluation protocol across subjects: While SKIM introduces data for five subjects, the experimental section does not clarify whether the reported numbers in Tables 2–4 represent an average across all five subjects or are restricted to a single representative subject.

strengths: Ambitious and novel problem setting: The paper addresses the challenging inverse problem of inferring 3D dynamic muscle anatomy deformations directly from visual surface observations and skeletal poses, bypassing expensive and inaccessible continuous medical imaging.

Well-engineered biomechanical regularization pipeline: The proposed decoupled formulation (structural muscle layer plus residual skin offset) is effectively constrained by biologically inspired priors—including tangential sliding resistance, biharmonic bending, and Gauss-Legendre quadrature-based signed volume preservation to prevent layer inversion and joint collapse.

High-fidelity data capture effort: The introduction of the SKIM dataset utilizes a high-density 120-camera capture studio, static full-body scanning, and a custom ArUco-embedded suit to track dense spatio-temporal skin correspondences across dynamic motions.

Clear ablation studies: The experimental section provides detailed ablation experiments verifying the necessity of each physical regularizer (volume preservation, biharmonic smoothing, tangential constraints) and comparing network architectures.
weaknesses: Lack of direct anatomical ground-truth validation during motion: Because in-vivo dynamic volumetric imaging (such as dynamic MRI or ultrasound) was not acquired during motion sequences, the accuracy of internal muscle deformation cannot be directly validated against real internal tissue dynamics; validation relies primarily on surface marker residuals and synthetic plausibility metrics (e.g., volume constancy, collision absence).

Pose-only conditioning without activation/load modeling: The model infers muscle deformation purely as a function of skeletal joint rotations r*(theta). In reality, muscle shape changes significantly with active muscle contraction, load, and co-contraction independent of joint angles (e.g., isometric flex vs. passive movement), which a purely kinematic pose-driven model cannot capture.

Reliance on heuristic template initialization: Rest-pose internal muscle and bone meshes are generated using heuristic volumetric fitting (Komaritzan et al., 2021) from surface scans rather than personalized medical scans. Any inaccuracies in resting muscle origins, insertions, or boundaries are baked into the pipeline and propagated during dynamic deformation.

Limited scalability and generalizability: The model is trained strictly per-subject and requires a specialized multi-camera setup with an ArUco suit, limiting its direct applicability to general in-the-wild video capture.

strengths: Compelling and novel problem setting: bridging dynamic multi-view visual observations with 3D internal muscle deformation in a data-driven framework, bypassing expensive FEM simulations at inference.

High-effort data acquisition: the SKIM dataset introduces dense tracking (over 2,300 ArUco markers per subject) captured across 120 synchronized cameras with resistance-training protocols across 5 subjects.

Principled mathematical formulation: the decoupled muscle-skin architecture and biomechanically inspired regularizers—particularly the exact signed volume calculation of triangular prisms via Gauss-Legendre quadrature and tangential sliding constraints—are well-motivated and technically sound.
Thorough ablation study and clear exposition: the ablations clearly isolate the necessity of both the vector regularizations and the volumetric/elastic physical priors.
weaknesses: Lack of internal ground-truth validation: Because dynamic in-vivo imaging (e.g., cine-MRI or dynamic ultrasound) is absent, the internal muscle deformation is evaluated via proxy physical plausibility metrics (volume preservation, layer non-penetration) rather than true underlying anatomical accuracy.

Purely pose-dependent deformation: The networks take only the kinematic skeletal pose features as input. However, muscle bulging and soft-tissue deformation vary significantly under isometric contraction, varying external loads, and fatigue—factors present in the recorded weighted resistance dataset but unaddressed by a purely pose-driven formulation.
Person-specific scope: The model must be trained per subject using individualized scanned templates and dense marker capture, limiting out-of-the-box applicability to unseen individuals.

Baseline comparisons: Comparing against HIT (which operates on generic SMPL topology without dataset-specific fine-tuning) naturally leads to disproportionately large errors (e.g., 115 mm MPME). Comparing against standard data-driven pose-corrective blendshape baselines (e.g., SNARF, Fast-SNARF, or SoftSMPL-style models) for surface fidelity would provide a more rigorous benchmark.

strengths: Addresses an important and challenging problem at the intersection of computer vision and biomechanics: inferring dynamic internal muscle deformation directly from external surface observations without requiring invasive dynamic medical imaging or prohibitive FEM simulations.

Introduces the SKIM dataset, captured with a dense 120-camera setup and a custom 2,310-marker ArUco suit across 5 subjects performing structured resistance routines, providing high-quality spatio-temporal surface deformation data.

Formulates a principled decoupled deformation framework that separates structural muscle deformation from subcutaneous skin sliding/compression, effectively avoiding the classic volumetric collapse (candy-wrapper artifact) of standard LBS.

The biomechanical regularizers are well-designed and mathematically sound, particularly the formulation of exact signed prism volumes via Gauss-Legendre quadrature to enforce volume preservation and penalize layer inversions.
The paper is clearly structured and provides thorough ablations validating the architectural choices and individual regularizers.
weaknesses: The ground-truth internal muscle anatomy is derived from static volumetric template fitting heuristics (Komaritzan et al. [33]) rather than true in-vivo volumetric imaging (e.g., dynamic MRI/ultrasound). Consequently, while external skin deformation is grounded in physical marker measurements, internal muscle deformation cannot be verified against true biological internal ground truth.

Muscle deformations are driven purely by kinematic joint angles $\boldsymbol{\theta}$. In physical resistance exercises, muscle bulging and activation vary dramatically with load, force generation, and voluntary co-contraction at identical joint angles; these dynamics cannot be resolved by skeletal pose alone.

The proposed framework is strictly subject-specific, requiring customized template fitting and extensive multi-view marker-suit capture per subject, which limits immediate applicability to general in-the-wild video capture.

The baseline comparisons are somewhat narrow. Comparing against HIT (an uncoupled implicit method trained on SMPL) naturally yields large cross-topology alignment errors (115 mm MPME). It would strengthen the paper to also compare against standard dynamic neural skin blendshape models (e.g., trained directly on the surface markers) to demonstrate whether incorporating the explicit internal muscle layer improves skin surface fidelity.

strengths: Tackles an ambitious and largely unexplored problem: recovering layered dynamic muscle deformations directly from external surface motion observations.

Introduction of the SKIM dataset, which is captured in a 120-camera multi-view studio with a custom suit containing 2,310 ArUco markers across 5 subjects performing varied resistance exercises, providing valuable dense surface correspondence data.

Principled mathematical formulation of the deformation priors, particularly the closed-form signed volume calculation using 2-point Gauss-Legendre quadrature over prismatic elements between anatomical layers.

Comprehensive ablation study (Tables 3 and 4) validating the contribution of each geometric prior (biharmonic bending, tangential sliding, incompressibility) and confirming the benefits of the U-Net architecture over MLPs and linear formulations.
weaknesses: Lack of direct internal dynamic ground truth: Because in-vivo dynamic volumetric imaging (such as dynamic MRI or ultrasound) is not available, the validation of internal muscle deformation relies entirely on surface marker tracking and physics-inspired surrogate metrics. As a result, the accuracy of the underlying individual muscle shapes remains largely an assumption driven by the geometric priors rather than empirical measurement.

Subject-specific limitation and scalability: The model must be trained individually per subject using data acquired from a high-end 120-camera capture studio and a custom physical marker suit. The framework does not provide cross-subject generalization or a shared parametric muscle space.

Limited dynamic baselines: The quantitative evaluation primarily compares against naive standard Linear Blend Skinning (LBS) and HIT (Keller et al., 2024). HIT was designed for static pose estimation from SMPL rather than dynamic multi-view tracking, which heavily skews the tracking metrics in Table 2 (115 mm vs. 13 mm) and makes it a weak point of comparison for dynamic soft-tissue deformations.

Resolution and readability of qualitative visualizations: In Figures 1, 6, and 7 (and supplementary Fig. 4 and 5), the color-coded displacement maps and muscle geometries are rendered at very small scales, making it difficult to clearly discern fine structural details, layer interpenetration, and individual muscle boundaries.
